clinicalPearls: Sarcocystis species are coccidian parasites with a two-host cycle, and humans can act either as the definitive (intestinal) host or as an accidental intermediate (muscular) host

Intestinal sarcocystosis follows eating raw or undercooked beef (Sarcocystis hominis) or pork (Sarcocystis suihominis) containing tissue cysts, causing self-limiting nausea, abdominal pain and diarrhoea
Muscular sarcocystosis follows ingesting oocysts from food or water contaminated by the faeces of the definitive carnivore host, leading to cyst formation in human muscle
Muscular disease presents with myalgia, fever, transient tender muscle swellings and eosinophilia, and has occurred in travellers to Southeast Asia in outbreak form
Intestinal infection is diagnosed by finding sporocysts or oocysts in stool, whereas muscular infection is confirmed by demonstrating sarcocysts on muscle biopsy
Raised creatine kinase and peripheral eosinophilia support a diagnosis of muscular disease
Intestinal disease usually needs only supportive care, while symptomatic muscular disease is managed supportively, with cotrimoxazole or antiparasitic agents sometimes tried
reference.pathophysiology: Sarcocystis has an obligatory predator-prey life cycle. When humans eat undercooked meat containing mature tissue cysts, the parasite completes sexual reproduction in the intestinal wall and sporocysts are shed in the stool, producing intestinal sarcocystosis. When humans instead ingest sporocysts shed by another carnivore, the parasite behaves as if in an intermediate host: released sporozoites disseminate haematogenously and encyst in skeletal and cardiac muscle, causing muscular sarcocystosis. The intramuscular cysts and the inflammatory, often eosinophilic, response to them account for the myalgia, muscle swelling and enzyme release seen in the muscular form, while intestinal invasion produces a milder self-limiting enteritis.
additionalDifferentials: Other coccidian enteric infections such as cystoisosporiasis
Toxocariasis and other causes of eosinophilic myositis
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for sporocysts or oocysts in intestinal disease
Skeletal muscle biopsy demonstrating sarcocysts in muscular disease
Serum creatine kinase and inflammatory markers
Full blood count for peripheral eosinophilia
Magnetic resonance imaging of affected muscle groups
Travel and dietary history to identify exposure
redFlags: Severe or persistent myositis with marked creatine kinase elevation
Cardiac involvement suggested by chest symptoms or troponin rise
Systemic illness with high fever and recurrent muscle swellings
Clustering of cases among travellers suggesting a common source outbreak
reference.prognosis: Intestinal sarcocystosis is self-limiting; muscular sarcocystosis tends to run a relapsing but ultimately self-limiting course over weeks to months, though prolonged myalgia can cause considerable morbidity.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish intestinal from muscular disease, which differ in exposure, presentation and diagnosis
Overlooking sarcocystosis in a traveller with fever, myalgia and eosinophilia
Relying on stool testing to diagnose muscular disease, in which stool is typically negative
Missing dietary history of raw or undercooked meat
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Manage intestinal disease supportively with oral rehydration and antiemetics, as the enteritis is self-limiting and needs no specific antiparasitic
For symptomatic muscular disease use non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and, in severe inflammatory reactions, corticosteroids to control myalgia and muscle swelling
Consider a trial of an anticoccidial agent such as co-trimoxazole or albendazole in troublesome muscular disease, recognising that curative antiparasitic treatment is unproven
Advise thorough cooking of beef and pork and access to clean, uncontaminated food and water to prevent both intestinal and muscular infection
Monitor creatine kinase and eosinophilia through the relapsing muscular course and reassure patients that resolution is expected over weeks to months
Refer to infectious diseases or tropical medicine for confirmed or outbreak-associated muscular disease
